title: Cut rents by 40% by law
detail: An emergency law to cut rents by 40% for current contracts, renewals and new contracts. The new rent would be the old rent minus 40%, but not lower than 60% of the local average. Homes not rented before would start at 60% of the local average.
c: A 40% cut in current contracts breaks agreed contracts and the right to property (art. 33 of the Constitution). Germany's Constitutional Court cancelled Berlin's rent limit in 2021, because the state of Berlin had no power to pass it. In our estimate, even if it passed, many owners would stop renting long-term.

s.t: Hahn, Kholodilin, Waltl, Fongoni, Management Science 70 (2024): the Berlin rent freeze

title: Ban buying homes you will not live in
detail: A ban on buying and collecting homes that are not used as a permanent home. For 4 years, a home you buy must be the main home of the buyer or a close relative, or the buyer's own second home. It cannot be left empty or rented out, except in a few cases such as social rental or moving for work. On the islands, extra limits for people who do not live there, whatever their nationality.
c: A general ban on buying homes except to live in them goes against arts. 33 and 38 of the Constitution and the EU rule on free movement of money. In our estimate it would hurt many small owners whose second flat is their savings.

title: Ban tourist flats
detail: End tourist use of flats in residential buildings (*vivienda turística*) while the housing emergency lasts. Current licences would end step by step, with no new ones. Illegal tourist flats would go, for free, to a public housing company. No new hotel beds in areas with mass tourism, with no end date.
c: As with Sumar, the regions and town halls give licences, and the state does not have this power. Tourism is one of Spain's largest industries, so expect conflict with the regions and with businesses.

title: Put short-term and room rentals under rental law
detail: Short-term rentals (*alquiler de temporada*) and room rentals would come under the Urban Leases Law (*LAU*) at once, so landlords cannot use them to avoid rent limits.
c: Closing this gap is a simple change to the LAU, and PSOE supports it too. It is realistic.
pos: It closes the gap that landlords use to avoid rent limits.
neg: It becomes harder for students and workers who move often to find temporary housing.

title: Make the large fortunes tax permanent
detail: Apply the tax on large fortunes to everyone who must pay wealth tax (*Impuesto del Patrimonio*), so regions cannot cancel it. The temporary solidarity tax (*ITSGF*) would become a permanent state tax with the same rules. Shares in family-run companies would no longer be tax-free above €100 million.
c: The solidarity tax already does this for fortunes above €3 million. Making it permanent is realistic by ordinary law. Regions run by PP will be against it.
pos: Regions cannot bring wealth tax down to zero, so there is less tax competition between them.
neg: In our estimate, it gives rich people a reason to move their money abroad. It brings in only a modest amount.

s.t: Ley 38/2022: solidarity tax on large fortunes, bank and energy levies (BOE)

title: End the Beckham law
detail: Fully end the special regime (*Ley Beckham*) that lets people who move to Spain to work pay much less tax than other taxpayers for 6 years.
c: An ordinary law is enough. The downside is that Spain loses a way to attract specialists, and several EU countries have similar regimes.
pos: All taxpayers are treated the same, and the state gets more tax money.
neg: It is harder for Spain to attract specialists and managers, because other countries offer similar tax breaks.

title: Lower VAT on everyday services
detail: 10% VAT on hairdressers. 10%, later 4%, on vets. 5% instead of 10% on tickets for theatre, dance, circus and concerts. A lower rate for artists who work through co-ops (21% today). No VAT on period products.
c: EU rules allow lower rates on these services. The cost is small.
pos: Everyday services, such as vets and hairdressers, become cheaper.
neg: The state loses tax money, and VAT cuts rarely reach prices in full.

title: Leave NATO and close the US bases at Rota and Morón
detail: Try to leave NATO (*OTAN*) by leaving the North Atlantic Treaty, and end the US military presence in Spain, including the Rota navy base and the Morón air base.
c: Leaving the treaty is possible (art. 13) if parliament agrees (arts. 94 and 96.2 of the Constitution). A referendum is not required and would only be advisory (art. 92), as in 1986. Congress will not vote to leave, because PSOE, PP and Vox are against. The bases are based on a separate treaty with the US.

title: Minimum wage up to €1,800 a month
detail: Raise the minimum wage (*SMI*) to €1,800 a month within four years, and set it by law at no less than 75% of the median wage.
c: The government sets the SMI by decision, so it is technically simple. But going from €1,221 (14 payments, 2026) to €1,800 in four years is a rise of almost 50%. Banco de España found that after the 2019 rise, jobs for low earners grew more slowly.

s.t: Real Decreto 126/2026: 2026 minimum wage of €1,221 a month (BOE)
Banco de España, Occasional Paper 2113 (2021): effects of the 2019 SMI rise

title: A 30-hour working week with the same pay
detail: Cut the working week to 30 hours within four years, starting with 35. A four-day week where the job allows it, and two days of working from home a week wherever possible.
c: Even 37.5 hours failed in Congress in 2025. As far as we know, no EU country has moved to 30 hours with no loss of pay in four years.

s.t: Congress, BOCG 15-A-58-3: 37.5-hour bill returned to the government (10 Sep 2025)

title: Lower the retirement age to 63
detail: Lower the normal retirement age (*jubilación*) to 63, and keep pensions safe and high enough with money from the state budget.
c: In our estimate, retirement at 63, while people live longer, would cost 2 to 3% of GDP more each year. It goes against Spain's promises to the EU to keep pensions affordable.

title: End the upper limit on social security fees
detail: End the maximum salary on which social security is paid (*base máxima de cotización*), and bring in fees that rise with income and company profits.
c: The maximum has been going up since 2023. Ending it while pensions keep their upper limit would turn the fees into a tax. Businesses are against it.
pos: More money for social security, and high earners pay a larger share.
neg: It is expensive for high earners and gives employers a reason to pay them in other ways. High earners would pay more without getting a higher pension, because pensions still have an upper limit.

s.t: Real Decreto-ley 2/2023: pension reform, MEI and contribution cap (BOE)

title: Citizenship after 1 year, the vote and a Spanish ID card
detail: Everyone who lives and works in Spain should get a Spanish ID card (*DNI*) and the right to vote. Change art. 22 of the Civil Code so that people who prove *arraigo* (ties to Spain) need only one year of residence. End the fees that make regularisation and citizenship harder.
c: In our estimate, citizenship after one year would be faster than almost anywhere in the EU. Giving foreigners the vote in general elections needs a change to the Constitution (art. 13.2).

title: A permanent way to get legal status
detail: A permanent way to get legal status based on social, family and community ties, not only a job contract. More kinds of proof that a person lives in Spain (*padrón*, travel passes, medical records), as in the special regularisation of 2026. Permits would renew automatically when the office is late and the person meets the conditions.
c: As with Sumar: a government that wants this route could make it by royal decree, as it did for the 2026 regularisation (RD 316/2026). PP and Vox are against it. A later government could undo a decree the same way. We rate it B because offices would need many more staff for the applications, as in 2026.
pos: Fewer people work without contracts, so the state gets more tax and social security payments, and workers are exploited less.
neg: A permanent route may attract more people to come (experts disagree on how many). It also puts a lot of pressure on offices, as in the 2026 regularisation (1.17 million applications).

s.t: Real Decreto 316/2026 on the 2026 regularisation, changing the immigration regulation (BOE)
La Moncloa, 2 Jul 2026: 1,174,978 regularisation applications filed
